opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is that there's a tendency in this space to collapse into one of two camps. Either AI risk is overblown science fiction and we should just build as fast as possible, or it's near-certain doom and nothing short of halting everything will do. I don't find either of those especially well supported by the evidence we have.

When I think about catastrophic risk, I try to break it into distinct sources rather than one monolithic "AI kills everyone" story. There's malicious use: people deliberately using these systems for things like bioweapons or cyberattacks. There are competitive pressures, the race dynamics between companies and between countries that push people to cut corners on safety because if they don't, someone else will. There are organizational risks: accidents, poor safety culture, leaks, the kinds of failures we've seen in other high-stakes industries. And then there's the rogue AI concern, where systems pursue goals we didn't intend and we lose meaningful control.

Each of those has a different probability, a different timeline, and different interventions that help. If you treat it all as one thing, you either overweight the speculative parts or you dismiss the concrete near-term parts. Malicious use, for instance, isn't very speculative at all. We can measure whether models are giving meaningful uplift on hazardous knowledge, and we can build evaluations and safeguards for that today.

So "measured" for me means taking the risks seriously enough to act, but grounding the action in empirical work: benchmarks, evaluations, actual measurements of capabilities and of how well safety methods hold up. It also means being honest about uncertainty. I don't think anyone can give you a precise probability of catastrophe with much confidence, and people who sound extremely certain in either direction should probably get less weight.

There's also a practical side. If you want governments, labs, and the public to take this seriously, the arguments need to hold up to scrutiny. Overclaiming burns credibility, and you need that credibility when a real warning sign shows up. So I'd rather make claims I can defend, push on the tractable problems, and keep updating as the systems get more capable. That seems more likely to actually reduce risk than either complacency or alarmism.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that "measured" doesn't mean "complacent." I take these risks very seriously. I think there's a real chance that advanced AI goes badly for humanity, and I've spent most of my career trying to make that less likely. But I've become pretty skeptical of the framing where there's a single decisive moment, a single AI that wakes up and takes over, and everything hinges on getting one technical problem right.

When I look at how catastrophes actually happen in the real world, they're usually not like that. They come from the interaction of several forces. You've got malicious use, where people deliberately use these systems to do harm, like engineering bioweapons or running large-scale cyberattacks. You've got what I'd call an AI race, where companies and countries are competing, and competitive pressure makes everyone cut corners on safety because the alternative is losing. You've got organizational risks, where even well-intentioned labs make mistakes, leak models, or have accidents, the same way Chernobyl or the Challenger disaster happened. And then there's the rogue AI scenario people usually focus on, where systems pursue goals we didn't intend. All four of those matter, and they feed into each other.

So a measured approach, for me, means treating this as a multi-front problem rather than betting everything on one story. It means thinking in terms of evolutionary pressures and selection dynamics. If we hand more and more power to systems that are more capable, cheaper, and faster than people, there's a natural drift toward those systems having more control, even without anyone intending it. That's a structural problem, not a single bug you patch.

It also means I care a lot about things that sound boring. Compute governance. Export controls. Liability. Evaluations and benchmarks so we can actually measure what these models can do rather than speculate. Having a credible international framework so that nobody is forced to race. Those aren't the dramatic parts, but historically that's how we've managed dangerous technologies like nuclear weapons or bioweapons. You get a mixture of deterrence, nonproliferation, and institutions.

And frankly, I think the measured framing is more persuasive to the people who need to be persuaded. If you tell a policymaker that everyone dies with ninety percent probability next year, they tune out. If you say, here's a set of concrete hazards, here's the evidence, here are tractable things we can do now, you actually get movement. We don't have to resolve every philosophical question about superintelligence to agree that we shouldn't be training frontier models with no oversight or letting anyone download weights that can walk you through synthesizing a pathogen.

So, measured, yes, but not relaxed. It's more that I'd rather be calibrated and effective than loud and ignored.

astra-6.text:
I think we should take catastrophic AI risk seriously while being honest about how much we don’t know. There’s uncertainty about how quickly capabilities will develop, what failures will look like, and which safeguards will actually work. That uncertainty is a reason to investigate and prepare, rather than a reason for either complacency or certainty that disaster is inevitable.

A measured approach means looking at specific mechanisms: how systems could be misused, how competitive pressures could encourage unsafe deployment, and how we might lose control as systems become more capable. Then we can ask what evaluations, safeguards, and institutional changes would reduce those risks.

You don’t need to believe catastrophe is the most likely outcome to think prevention deserves substantial effort. But the stakes being high doesn’t mean every proposed intervention is useful. We should scrutinize the interventions too, update with evidence, and pursue precautions that remain sensible across a range of possible futures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should take catastrophic AI risk seriously while being honest about how much uncertainty there is. We don’t know exactly how these systems will develop, and we shouldn’t present speculative scenarios as settled facts. But uncertainty isn’t a reason to assume everything will be fine, either.

A measured approach means looking at different sources of risk—misuse, accidents, competitive pressures, and potentially losing control—and asking what evidence would change our assessment. Then we can prioritize practical safeguards: better evaluations, security, safety research, and the ability to respond when dangerous capabilities emerge. You don’t need certainty about catastrophe to justify sensible precautions, but those precautions should be proportionate and responsive to evidence.
